_note: Quiz and true-or-false items written but not yet blind-checked; apply_check.py moves checked items onto the site.

item.statement: Research has shown that smoking weed doesn't raise lung cancer risk.
item.why: Pooled studies found no clear link, but a higher risk couldn't be ruled out. A Swedish study found about twice the rate in men who'd used cannabis over 50 times, though nearly all of them also smoked tobacco.

item.statement: Once THC is gone from your blood, the effects are over.
item.why: In one lab study of 17 people, after the higher amount, people still rated an effect when their blood THC was back to zero.

item.statement: Young adults who vape weed report more cough and phlegm than those who never have.
item.why: In one survey, about 1 in 4 who'd vaped cannabis in the past month reported a lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis, against 1 in 8 who never had. It's what people said, so it can't show cause.

item.statement: Most people hurt in the 2019 vaping lung outbreak said they had vaped THC.
item.why: Of 2,022 US patients who said what they'd vaped, 82 in 100 named a THC product and 14 in 100 only nicotine. Nobody checked their devices.

item.statement: Vitamin E acetate has been proven to cause the 2019 vaping lung injuries.
item.why: It was in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients and none of 99 healthy people, but no study tested whether it causes the injury, and other chemicals aren't ruled out.

item.statement: Most ER visits for being too high on weed follow edibles.
item.why: At one Colorado hospital, 647 of 762 such visits followed smoking or vaping, and edibles were about 1 in 11 of all its cannabis visits. These are shares of visits, not risks.

item.statement: In one ER, heart symptoms came up more often after edibles than after smoking or vaping.
item.why: At one US hospital, heart symptoms came up in 8 in 100 edible visits, against 3 in 100 smoking or vaping visits. Nobody counted how much people had taken.

item.statement: The THC number on an edible's label is usually right.
item.why: In a 2014 test of 75 US edibles, only 17 in 100 were within a tenth of their label; 60 in 100 held less and 23 in 100 more. It's one test, not picked at random.

item.statement: Most studies that report THC strength used cannabis as strong as what's sold now.
item.why: In a review of 452 such studies for Colorado, the typical strength studied was well below what's sold now, its authors say. Only 54 looked directly at concentrates and health.

item.statement: In most studies, people who use stronger weed show more signs of a use disorder.
item.why: In four of six studies, people who used stronger cannabis, like skunk, had more signs of a use disorder. All took people's word for how strong it was, and none could show cause.

item.statement: Taking 5-HTP before or after ecstasy has been shown to protect the brain.
item.why: Whether any of it lowers harm wasn't studied, and the authors say evidence for taking things beforehand comes only from rodents given injections. They warn that 5-HTP with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.
